column1: # The target column is deliberately empty, and this is the first dictionary in
# en-es.tsv and en-uz.tsv carry a hand-authored or hand-checked translation for
# every row. Nobody on this project reads Chinese, so authoring 539 of them by
# hand would have meant either machine-translating them into a file that then
# *looks* hand-checked, or shipping the placeholder rows en-uz still carries —
# `the -> the`, the English left in the target column, which is the worst of the
# three because it is indistinguishable from a real answer.
# So the file carries only what it actually knows: which English words earn a
# dictionary entry and in what order. That is the whole English side of
# en-es.tsv — the same OpenSubtitles-2018 frequency ordering, the same
# lemma reduction by the extension's own lemmatizer, the same phrase section at
# the same hand-placed ranks — and it is genuinely language-independent data,
# The Chinese is filled in by `Linguaswap.Dictionary`, which only ever supplies
# a translation that is missing, and is then checked by
# `Linguaswap.Verification` before it is served to anyone. An entry with an
# empty target column is kept out of the active pool and out of the API until
# that has happened, so importing this file changes nothing a user sees.
# Chinese does not inflect, so no entry here will ever carry `forms`. What it
# carries instead is `pronunciation` — pinyin with tone marks — because a reader
# who meets 跑 on a page has no way to sound it out, and a gloss they cannot say
